title: TCP and UDP
subtitle: IP delivers packets when it feels like it. TCP turns that into a reliable, ordered stream, and learns how fast it may go.

sections.title: Process-to-process delivery
sections.body:
The postman delivers a letter to your building. But who in the building should open it? The network layer gets a packet to a host; the transport layer gets it to a process. A 16-bit port number identifies the process, and the pair (IP, port) is a socket. The sender multiplexes many applications onto one network connection; the receiver demultiplexes by port.

You have two flavours to choose from. UDP adds only ports and a checksum: fast, connectionless, no guarantees (DNS, streaming, games). TCP adds connections, reliability, ordering, flow and congestion control (web, email, files). Why would an application choose UDP? When speed and low delay matter more than perfect delivery, as in a live call.

questions.prompt: Why would an application choose UDP?

choices.text: It wants low latency and no connection set-up, and can tolerate or handle loss itself.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: DNS queries and live video do not want to wait for retransmissions.

keynotes: The network layer gets a packet to a host; the transport layer gets it to a process by a 16-bit port number, and (IP, port) is a socket.
The sender multiplexes many applications onto one network connection; the receiver demultiplexes by port.
UDP adds only ports and a checksum (DNS, streaming, games); TCP adds connections, reliability, ordering, flow and congestion control (web, email, files).

sections.title: The three-way handshake
sections.body:
Before two people talk seriously on the phone, they check: “Can you hear me?” “Yes, can you hear me?” “Yes.” TCP does the same with its three-way handshake. Before data flows it agrees initial sequence numbers: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client ACKs. Teardown uses FIN and ACK in each direction (a four-step close), since each side closes its half independently.

Press Simulate to watch the segments cross. Why three messages rather than two? Because both sides must confirm that they can send and hear, and two messages would only prove one direction.

questions.prompt: Why three messages rather than two?

choices.text: Both sides must learn the other’s initial sequence number and confirm it was received.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Two messages would leave the server unsure that the client got its SYN-ACK.

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — TCP connection life cycle
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Client] as c
[Server] as s
c -> s : SYN, seq = x
s --> c : SYN-ACK, seq = y, ack = x+1
c -> s : ACK, ack = y+1

s --> c : ACK

s --> c : ACK + FIN
c -> s : ACK");

keynotes: Before data flows TCP agrees initial sequence numbers: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, the client ACKs.
Teardown uses FIN and ACK in each direction, a four-step close, since each side closes its half independently.
The three messages let both sides confirm they can send and receive.

sections.title: Reliability and flow control
sections.body:
How does TCP promise you that every byte arrives, in order, even over an unreliable network? By numbering. TCP numbers every byte. The receiver’s acknowledgement is cumulative (“I have everything up to byte N”). Loss is detected by a timeout or by three duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit).

The receiver also advertises a window, the free space in its buffer, and the sender never has more than that outstanding: flow control stops a fast sender overrunning a slow receiver. It is the sliding window of the previous chapter, applied to a byte stream. Say a receiver advertises a 4000-byte window and the sender has sent bytes 1000–2999 unacknowledged. It may send 4000 − 2000 = 2000 more bytes. Three duplicate ACKs signal that a segment was probably lost.

worked.why: A receiver advertises a 4000-byte window; the sender has sent bytes 1000–2999 unacknowledged.

choices.text: A probably lost segment — retransmit without waiting for the timeout.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Later segments are arriving, so only one is missing.

keynotes: TCP numbers every byte, and acknowledgements are cumulative (“I have everything up to byte N”).
Loss is detected by a timeout or by three duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit).
A 4000-byte advertised window with 2000 bytes in flight lets the sender send 2000 more; flow control stops a fast sender overrunning a slow receiver.

sections.title: Congestion control
sections.body:
Flow control protects the receiver. But who protects the network from you and everyone sending too fast? Congestion control does, and TCP does it by feeling its way, like someone testing bathwater. TCP keeps a congestion window cwnd. Slow start: cwnd doubles each RTT from 1 until it reaches ssthresh. Congestion avoidance: +1 segment per RTT.

When trouble comes: on three duplicate ACKs, Reno halves the threshold and continues from there (fast recovery); Tahoe restarts from 1. A timeout sends both back to 1. The saw-tooth is the signature of TCP. In the first figure, Reno grows, loses a packet at RTT 9, and then halves; in the second, Tahoe restarts from 1 after the same loss. During slow start, cwnd grows exponentially, doubling every round trip.

questions.prompt: During slow start, how does cwnd grow?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each ACK adds one segment, so a full window of ACKs doubles the window.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Then it would never probe the capacity.

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.1 — TCP Reno
figures.note: Reno: growth, a loss at RTT 9, then halving.

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.2 — TCP Tahoe
figures.note: Tahoe restarts from 1 after the same loss.

problems.prompt: Reno with ssthresh 8 and a 3-dup-ACK loss at RTT 9: list cwnd for the first 16 RTTs (Tahoe too).
problems.answer: Reno: 1 2 4 8 9 10 11 12 13 6 7 8 9 10 11 12. Tahoe: 1 2 4 8 9 10 11 12 13 1 2 4 6 7 8 9. Reno resumes at half the window; Tahoe falls back to slow start.

keynotes: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network, using the congestion window cwnd.
Slow start doubles cwnd each RTT from 1 until ssthresh; congestion avoidance adds 1 segment per RTT.
On three duplicate ACKs Reno halves the threshold and continues (fast recovery) while Tahoe restarts from 1; a timeout sends both back to 1.

sections.title: Sockets
sections.body:
A socket is your handle on all this machinery as a programmer. A server calls socket → bind → listen → accept and then recv/send; a client calls socket → connect then send/recv. The figure shows the call order on each side.

One subtlety pays off the first time you write a server. accept returns a new socket for each client while the listening socket keeps waiting, like a receptionist who hands each visitor to a colleague and returns to the desk.

choices.text: A new socket dedicated to the connecting client.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It returns a socket (address available separately).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The original listening socket remains open for more clients.

figures.caption: Figure 5.5.1 — socket calls
figures.note: The call order on each side.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Client] as c
[Server] as s
s -> s : socket, bind, listen
c -> c : socket
c -> s : connect, then handshake
s -> s : accept → new socket
c -> s : send(request)
s --> c : send(response)
c -> s : close");

keynotes: A server calls socket, bind, listen and accept, then recv/send.
A client calls socket and connect, then send/recv.
accept returns a new socket for each client while the listening socket keeps waiting.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Three lines to keep.

  • Ports pick processes; TCP = reliable stream, UDP = datagrams.
  • Handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
  • Flow control = receiver’s window; congestion control = cwnd (slow start, AIMD).
keynotes: Ports pick processes; TCP is a reliable stream and UDP is datagrams.
The handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
Flow control uses the receiver’s window; congestion control uses cwnd (slow start, AIMD).
